name: Concatenating Strings and Numbers (Case 3)
description: Construct a program that uses variables x, y, and z to print "10 + 20 = 30".
code:
#Step 1: Assign initial values to the variables x, y, and z
x = 10
y = 20
z = x + y
#Step 2: Print the text using the variables initialized above 
print(str(x) + " + " + str(y) + " = " + str(z))

1.content: #Step 1: Assign initial values to the variables x, y, and z

commentList: You assign the number 10 to the variable x so the program has a concrete value to use in later calculations and printing.
You are using three parts here: x (the variable name), = (the assignment operator), and 10 (an integer literal); together they make x hold the integer 10.
You must do this before you compute z = x + y — without this assignment x would be undefined and the addition would fail.
Be careful not to use == by mistake; x == 10 is a comparison and does not store a value. Also avoid x = "10" if you want x to be a number rather than a string.
For readability follow the style x = 10 with spaces around =, and in larger programs prefer more descriptive names than single letters so you (and others) can understand the code later.
If you need to change the value, you simply assign again (for example, x = 15). Make sure x stays a numeric type when you plan to do arithmetic with it.
Purpose: You give the name y the value 20 so it becomes the second number in the addition and the text output "10 + 20 = 30".
Syntax: 'y = 20' is an assignment statement — the variable name y appears on the left and the expression 20 (an integer literal) is placed on the right; the = operator stores that value in y.
How it works: After this line runs, you can use y in expressions like z = x + y; Python will treat y as the integer 20 when performing the addition.

Common mistakes: If you write y = "20" (with quotes) y becomes a string and x + y will raise a TypeError because you cannot add an int and a str. Also using '==' instead of '=' will not assign a value (it’s a comparison), and using y before assigning it causes a NameError.
Best practices: Put spaces around the = for readability (y = 20), choose clear variable names for larger programs, and keep the variable's type consistent when you plan numeric operations.
You compute and store the result: z = x + y evaluates the sum of x and y and assigns that numerical result to z so z will be 30 given x = 10 and y = 20.
You can read the syntax as 'assign to z the value of x plus y': Python first evaluates x + y (arithmetic addition because x and y are integers) and then stores that value in the variable named z.

Be careful: + can mean different things depending on types—if x and y were strings you'd get string concatenation ('10' + '20' -> '1020'), and if one is a string while the other is an int you'd get a TypeError; make sure x and y hold numeric types when you want arithmetic.

Best practice: keep this calculation on its own line so the logic is clear, use descriptive variable names, and if you get values from input convert them with int(...) before adding to avoid type errors.

5.content: #Step 2: Print the text using the variables initialized above

commentList: You are printing the final formatted sentence '10 + 20 = 30' by sending one combined string to the console with print(...).
str(x), str(y), and str(z) convert the numeric values to text; the + operators here join those text pieces and the literal pieces ' + ' and ' = ' into one continuous string.
If you omit the str(...) calls, you will get a TypeError because Python does not let you concatenate a string and an integer with +; you must convert numbers to strings before joining them this way.
A common alternative is print(x, '+', y, '=', z) — print will convert values for you and add spaces automatically — or, for clearer and more modern code, use an f-string: print(f'{x} + {y} = {z}').
Remember that the addition happened on Line 4 (z = x + y); this line only formats and prints the already-computed result, so the order of operations matters.

Best practices: prefer readable formatting (f-strings or str.format), keep conversions explicit when concatenating, and avoid extra spaces in the literal pieces unless you want them shown exactly as output.

You might pick this line if you confuse the plus sign with the times sign or think 'combine' means to multiply. If you use this line, z will hold the product of x and y (10 * 20 = 200), so the program will print "10 + 20 = 200" — it runs without error but gives the wrong number. This distractor is wrong because it uses the multiplication operation instead of performing the numeric combination that the program needs; it changes the mathematical operation and so the printed result is incorrect.

commentList: Step-by-step why you might pick this: you probably expect the + operator to glue pieces together and assume Python will convert the numbers for you. That makes this look concise and natural. What actually happens if you use this line: Python will try to use + to join string parts and integer parts together and will raise a TypeError because you cannot concatenate a string and an int. So the program will crash and nothing will be printed. How this differs from a correct approach: here you're missing an explicit conversion of the numeric variables to text before concatenation. You might be influenced by other languages that do implicit conversion, but in this program that assumption makes the line invalid.

commentList: Why you might choose this: you converted the numbers to strings, then added z with a comma because you expect print to handle the last value automatically. What really happens: the first part is a single string that ends with a space, and the comma makes print treat z as a separate argument. print inserts a default separator (a space) between arguments, so the final output will have an extra space before the number (for example, '10 + 20 =  30' with two spaces). That means the printed text won't match the exact requested formatting. In short, mixing concatenation and a comma changes spacing in a way you may not expect, so the result is formatted incorrectly.
